interactions.label: Neurotrophins such as nerve growth factor are produced by target tissues in limi

params.question: Neurotrophins such as nerve growth factor are produced by target tissues in limited amounts. What is the developmental consequence of this limited supply?

answers.text: All neurons survive but form proportionally weaker synaptic connections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Limited neurotrophin supply does not weaken connections — it eliminates neurons entirely. Those that fail to capture enough trophic support undergo apoptosis during development.

answers.text: Neurons that fail to capture sufficient neurotrophic support undergo programmed cell death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Neurons compete for target-derived neurotrophins that bind Trk receptors on axon terminals and travel retrogradely to suppress the default cell-death programme. Losers of this competition are eliminated by apoptosis.

answers.text: Excess neurons migrate to alternative target tissues where neurotrophin is available

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postmitotic neurons cannot migrate to alternative targets. Those that fail to capture neurotrophic support from their designated target die by programmed cell death.

answers.text: Motor neurons compensate by synthesising their own neurotrophins at the soma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neurons depend on target-derived neurotrophins transported retrogradely to the soma. They cannot substitute with self-produced neurotrophins.

overallFeedback.feedback: Neurotrophins are target-derived and limited in supply. Neurons compete to capture them via Trk receptors; those that fail undergo programmed cell death during development, matching neuronal numbers to target tissue size.

Correct! Target-derived neurotrophins (NGF, BDNF) are limited, creating competition among innervating neurons. The receptor complex is retrogradely transported to suppress apoptosis — those that fail are eliminated during development.

interactions.label: The neuromuscular junction operates with a safety factor of three to four times

params.question: The neuromuscular junction operates with a safety factor of three to four times threshold. What does this safety factor signify for normal transmission?

answers.text: Each nerve impulse releases enough acetylcholine to fire three to four separate muscle action potentials

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The safety factor does not mean multiple action potentials per impulse. It means the end-plate potential far exceeds the single threshold needed, so transmission remains reliable even if some acetylcholine release is lost.

answers.text: The motor end plate has three to four backup receptor clusters that activate under high demand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There are no reserve receptor clusters. The safety factor arises because the quantal content of acetylcholine release generates an EPP well above the threshold needed to trigger a muscle action potential.

answers.text: The end-plate potential normally exceeds the threshold for a muscle action potential by three to four times, ensuring reliable transmission

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The EPP is three to four times above threshold, so every nerve impulse reliably triggers a muscle action potential. Diseases like myasthenia gravis must destroy enough of this reserve before weakness appears.

answers.text: The junction can transmit reliably at up to four times the normal maximum nerve firing frequency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The safety factor refers to EPP amplitude exceeding threshold, not to the range of firing frequencies the junction can handle.

overallFeedback.feedback: The safety factor means the end-plate potential normally exceeds the threshold for a muscle action potential by three to four times. Diseases must exhaust this reserve before transmission fails and weakness becomes apparent.

Correct! The EPP exceeds threshold by a factor of 3–4×. This reserve is why diseases such as myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome must substantially reduce transmission before clinical weakness appears.

interactions.label: During the sliding filament mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction, which stru

params.question: During the sliding filament mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction, which structural change occurs within the sarcomere?

answers.text: Both the I band and H zone narrow while the A band remains constant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. As actin filaments slide inward past myosin during the cross-bridge cycle, the I band (actin-only zone) and H zone (myosin-only zone) narrow. The A band stays the same because myosin length is unchanged.

answers.text: The A band shortens as the myosin filaments are compressed by actin sliding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The A band corresponds to the full length of the thick myosin filaments, which do not shorten or compress. The A band remains constant throughout contraction.

answers.text: Thin actin filaments contract and pull the Z lines closer together

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sliding filament model states that neither thick nor thin filaments shorten. The Z lines do move closer, but because actin slides past myosin — not because actin itself contracts.

answers.text: The Z lines move apart as the muscle develops isometric tension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Z lines move closer together during contraction, not apart. Even in isometric contraction, sarcomeres attempt to shorten internally while total muscle length is held constant.

overallFeedback.feedback: In the sliding filament mechanism, neither thick nor thin filaments shorten. As actin slides past myosin, the I band (actin-only) and H zone (myosin-only) narrow, while the A band (full myosin length) stays constant.
Correct! In the sliding filament mechanism, neither filament changes length. Actin slides inward past myosin, narrowing the I band and H zone while the A band remains constant.

interactions.label: Skeletal muscle force is graded by two mechanisms: recruitment and rate coding.

params.question: Skeletal muscle force is graded by two mechanisms: recruitment and rate coding. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?

answers.text: Recruitment increases the firing frequency of active motor units; rate coding activates additional motor units

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two mechanisms. Recruitment is the process of activating additional motor units; rate coding is the process of increasing the firing frequency of those already active.

answers.text: Recruitment operates only during isometric contraction; rate coding operates only during isotonic contraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both mechanisms operate together regardless of contraction type. The nervous system combines recruitment and rate coding to produce smoothly graded force for all voluntary movements.

answers.text: Recruitment and rate coding are two names for the same process of summating motor unit responses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: They are distinct mechanisms. Recruitment adds more motor units to the active pool; rate coding increases how rapidly each active motor unit fires, fusing twitches into sustained force.

answers.text: Recruitment activates motor units from smallest to largest as demand rises; rate coding increases the firing frequency of active units

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Recruitment follows the size principle, adding progressively larger motor units as force demand increases. Rate coding raises the firing rate of already-active units, producing summation and eventually smooth tetanus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recruitment activates motor units progressively from smallest to largest (the size principle). Rate coding increases the firing frequency of already-active units, producing summation and eventually tetanus. The two mechanisms work together to grade force.

Correct! Recruitment follows the size principle (small motor units first, large ones added as demand rises), and rate coding increases firing frequency to fuse twitches into smooth tetanus. Together they produce graded voluntary force.

interactions.label: Repetitive nerve stimulation is used to distinguish myasthenia gravis from Lambe

params.question: Repetitive nerve stimulation is used to distinguish myasthenia gravis from Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Which pair of findings correctly matches each condition?

answers.text: Myasthenia gravis: greater than 100% increment at 50 Hz; Lambert-Eaton: greater than 10% decrement at 3 Hz

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two findings. The increment belongs to Lambert-Eaton syndrome (presynaptic calcium accumulation at high frequency), and the decrement belongs to myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic receptor loss at low frequency).

answers.text: Myasthenia gravis: greater than 10% decrement at 2–3 Hz; Lambert-Eaton: greater than 100% increment at 20–50 Hz

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In myasthenia gravis, receptor destruction means successive EPPs fall below threshold during low-frequency stimulation, producing a decrement. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, calcium accumulates in the terminal during high-frequency stimulation, overcoming reduced release to produce an increment.

answers.text: Both conditions produce an identical decrement pattern at all stimulation frequencies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The RNS patterns are diagnostically distinct. Myasthenia gravis shows a decrement at low frequency, while Lambert-Eaton syndrome characteristically shows an increment at high frequency.

answers.text: Myasthenia gravis: normal response at all frequencies; Lambert-Eaton: decrement only at high frequency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Myasthenia gravis does produce an abnormal response — a characteristic decrement of greater than 10% at low-frequency stimulation. The response is distinctly abnormal, not normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: In myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic), low-frequency RNS at 2–3 Hz produces a greater than 10% decrement. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome (presynaptic), high-frequency RNS at 20–50 Hz produces a greater than 100% increment.

Correct! The decrement in MG reflects postsynaptic receptor destruction (fewer receptors available with each successive impulse), while the increment in LEMS reflects presynaptic calcium accumulation overcoming the reduced vesicle release per impulse.

interactions.label: Two subjects perform ergography with identical loads and lifting rates. Subject

params.question: Two subjects perform ergography with identical loads and lifting rates. Subject A shows a long plateau of consistent lift heights followed by a gradual decline. Subject B shows a steep decline from the first few lifts. What does this difference most likely reflect?

answers.text: Subject A has faster motor nerve conduction velocities

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nerve conduction velocity determines signal speed, not the endurance of repeated muscle contractions. The ergogram reflects the muscle fibre's metabolic capacity and resistance to fatigue.

answers.text: Subject B has a greater proportion of slow, fatigue-resistant Type I fibres

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A greater proportion of Type I fibres would improve endurance, producing a longer plateau — not a steep early decline. Subject B's pattern suggests the opposite.

answers.text: Subject A has greater muscle endurance, likely from training that enhances oxidative capacity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A long plateau indicates sustained force production before fatigue sets in, reflecting better training adaptation and greater oxidative capacity in the working muscle fibres.

answers.text: Subject B is exerting maximal voluntary effort on every lift while Subject A is pacing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both subjects lift at the same rate against the same load, so the protocol controls for effort differences. The difference lies in the muscle's intrinsic resistance to fatigue.

overallFeedback.feedback: The ergogram shape reflects the muscle's endurance profile. A trained subject shows a long plateau followed by a gradual decline. An early steep decline indicates rapid fatigue — the same mechanisms you studied in the muscle energy systems section.

Correct! The ergogram shape is a direct readout of the muscle's resistance to fatigue. A long plateau reflects trained, fatigue-resistant muscle; a steep decline reflects early fatigue from lower oxidative capacity.

interactions.label: In skeletal muscle, contraction is regulated by troponin on the thin filament, w

params.question: In skeletal muscle, contraction is regulated by troponin on the thin filament, whereas in smooth muscle it is regulated by calmodulin-dependent phosphorylation of the myosin head on the thick filament.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Skeletal muscle uses troponin on the thin filament as its regulatory switch, while smooth muscle uses the calcium–calmodulin–MLCK pathway to phosphorylate the myosin head on the thick filament. This difference is why smooth muscle produces slow, sustained contraction at very low energy cost.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. In skeletal muscle, calcium binds troponin C on the thin filament, shifting tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites on actin. In smooth muscle, calcium binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase to phosphorylate the myosin head — placing the regulatory switch on the thick filament instead.
